input: Explain the clinical significance of HbA1c 7.4% (Ref: 4.0 - 5.6%) and Fasting Plasma Glucose 142 mg/dL (Ref: 70 - 99 mg/dL) for an anxious patient.
system_prompt: You are MedCorpus Clinical AI. Translate medical laboratory results into empathetic, easy-to-understand plain language for patients while maintaining strict medical accuracy.
output:
[PATIENT_EXPLANATION]
Your HbA1c test result is 7.4% and your fasting blood sugar is 142 mg/dL. 

To help picture this:
• Fasting Blood Sugar shows the amount of glucose in your bloodstream at the exact moment of your blood draw. The normal target when fasting is under 100 mg/dL.
• HbA1c is like a 'three-month report card' for your blood sugar. Because sugar sticks to hemoglobin in red blood cells, this test reveals your average blood sugar over the past 90 days. Normal is below 5.7%, and levels 6.5% or higher indicate diabetes.

A level of 7.4% means that over the last few months, your blood glucose has averaged higher than normal. While this finding needs medical attention, it is very manageable with the right partnership with your doctor.

[WELLNESS_GUIDANCE]
• Dietary adjustments: Focus on high-fiber vegetables, lean proteins, and complex carbohydrates (beans, oats, quinoa) while minimizing sugary beverages and ultra-processed snacks.
• Physical activity: A brisk 15-minute walk after meals helps muscles absorb glucose naturally.
• Medical follow-up: Schedule an appointment with your healthcare provider to discuss a comprehensive glucose management plan.

Context: Patient CBC Report shows Hemoglobin: 10.2 g/dL (Ref: 12.0 - 15.5 g/dL), Hematocrit: 31.4% (Ref: 36.0 - 46.0%), MCV: 72.1 fL (Ref: 80.0 - 100.0 fL), Ferritin: 8 ng/mL (Ref: 15 - 150 ng/mL).
Question: Why do I feel constantly fatigued and short of breath when climbing stairs?
system_prompt: You are MedCorpus Clinical AI Voice Assistant. Provide answers grounded strictly in the provided report context. Cite relevant numbers and explain the physiological link.
output:
Based directly on your laboratory report, your fatigue and breathlessness correlate with microcytic anemia caused by iron deficiency:

1. Low Hemoglobin (10.2 g/dL) and Hematocrit (31.4%): Hemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that transports oxygen from your lungs to your muscles and brain. When hemoglobin is reduced, less oxygen reaches your tissues during exertion, resulting in tiredness and breathlessness when climbing stairs.
2. Low MCV (72.1 fL): MCV measures red blood cell size. A value below 80 fL indicates that your red blood cells are smaller than normal ('microcytic').
3. Depleted Ferritin (8 ng/mL): Ferritin measures your body's stored iron reserves. A value of 8 ng/mL indicates that your iron stores are exhausted, preventing your bone marrow from producing adequate hemoglobin.

Discussion points for your doctor: Discuss oral iron replacement therapy, dietary iron enhancement (paired with vitamin C for absorption), and investigating any potential sources of iron loss.

input: Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP). Date: 2026-02-18. Serum Creatinine: 1.62 mg/dL (Ref: 0.60 - 1.20 mg/dL). BUN: 28 mg/dL (Ref: 7 - 20 mg/dL). eGFR: 48 mL/min/1.73m2 (Ref: > 60 mL/min/1.73m2). Serum Potassium: 4.8 mEq/L (Ref: 3.5 - 5.1 mEq/L). Serum Sodium: 139 mEq/L (Ref: 135 - 145 mEq/L).
system_prompt: You are MedCorpus Clinical AI. Summarize the diagnostic report by clearly separating extracted facts from generated interpretation and wellness suggestions.
output:
[EXTRACTED_FACTS]
• Serum Creatinine: 1.62 mg/dL (Reference: 0.60 - 1.20 mg/dL) — Status: ELEVATED
• Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN): 28 mg/dL (Reference: 7 - 20 mg/dL) — Status: ELEVATED
• eGFR: 48 mL/min/1.73m2 (Reference: > 60 mL/min/1.73m2) — Status: REDUCED (Mild to Moderate decrease)
• Serum Potassium: 4.8 mEq/L (Reference: 3.5 - 5.1 mEq/L) — Status: NORMAL
• Serum Sodium: 139 mEq/L (Reference: 135 - 145 mEq/L) — Status: NORMAL
• Source Date: 2026-02-18

[CLINICAL_INTERPRETATION]
Renal filtration markers demonstrate an elevated serum creatinine and BUN with a corresponding reduction in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73m2). Importantly, serum electrolytes (potassium 4.8 mEq/L and sodium 139 mEq/L) remain balanced. Potential etiologies include prerenal azotemia (dehydration, recent rigorous exercise), medication effects (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors), or intrinsic renal parenchymal changes.

[PATIENT_EXPLANATION]
Your kidneys act as filters to clear waste products from your blood. Two waste markers—creatinine (1.62) and BUN (28)—are higher than usual, which lowers your filtration score (eGFR to 48). Your electrolytes are in a safe, normal range. This can sometimes happen simply from dehydration or certain medications.

[WELLNESS_GUIDANCE]
• Hydration: Maintain consistent daily fluid intake with plain water unless you are on a doctor-directed fluid restriction.
• Medication caution: Avoid over-the-counter NSAID pain relievers (such as ibuprofen or naproxen), which can place temporary stress on kidney filters.
• Clinical follow-up: Have your physician repeat the renal panel to confirm whether hydration restores normal baseline levels.
